newsitem.title: FINLAND: NATO - from Cold War warrior to Bosnia enforcer.
newsitem.headline: NATO - from Cold War warrior to Bosnia enforcer.

text.p: NATO, the main focus of the U.S.-Russian summit in Helsinki, was founded to defend the West in the Cold War but has since forged a new role by keeping the peace in Bosnia and preparing to expand into Eastern Europe.

Countries that were once part of the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact are now clamouring to join the 16-nation North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), which is led by the United States and offers nuclear-backed security guarantees to its members.

Founded in 1949, NATO was designed to stave off any Soviet attack. Its guiding principle of collective defence, enshrined in the Washington Treaty, is based on the idea that member states will come to the aid of any ally under attack.
The collapse of the Berlin Wall in 1989 left the alliance struggling to define its purpose, particularly while the West hesitated over the conflict in former Yugoslavia.
NATO's reputation was restored by major air strikes which helped bring an end to the Bosnian war in 1995 and by the alliance's decision to lead the 60,000-strong peace force there.
A dozen countries in Central and Eastern Europe, now democracies, are worried about their own security and have been asking to join. Russia sees this as a threat to its security.

The alliance is expected to invite several to start membership talks at a Madrid summit in July, with the aim that they will join in 1999. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic top the list of likely new members, although Slovenia and Romania may also be considered.

NATO has also promised to increase stability across Europe through its Partnership for Peace programme on military cooperation with all of its former foes, and is trying to build new forms of cooperation with Russia.
